title: Why is Energetic Particle Precipitation Important for Climate Research and Seasonal Forecasting?
abstract: Over the past decades, numerous observations and model studies have provided substantial evidence that energetic particle precipitation (EPP) affects the chemistry and dynamics of the stratosphere. Concurrently, the significance of stratospheric dynamics, particularly in winter short-range and seasonal forecasts, has been highlighted. However, there has been little effort to integrate the knowledge from these two research fields. This review aims to bridge the gap between the Space Physics and Climate research communities. It will elucidate current knowledge on EPP and its impact on the chemistry and dynamics of the mesosphere and stratosphere, highlighting recent research. Additionally, it will present scientific findings demonstrating that EPP induced changes in the mesosphere and stratosphere can migrate downwards into the troposphere and reach the surface. Particularly during the eastward phase of the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation and/or close to a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW), EPP can significantly impact stratospheric dynamics projected onto the North Atlantic Oscillation or Northern Annular Mode. The review highlights EPP as a potential moderator of SSWs in terms of their occurrence, timing, and strength, which are all crucial parameters for short-range and seasonal forecasts for the northern hemispheric winter. Moreover, it presents research demonstrating that the EPP chemical-dynamical coupling is becoming stronger in an atmosphere influenced by climate change. Bridging the gap between space physics and climate research is essential, as the natural variability of the atmosphere underpins the climate signal. Better prediction of SSWs and their effects on northern winter weather is crucial in preparing for extreme weather events and supporting economic activities. This interdisciplinary approach can enhance our overall understanding of the Earth’s atmosphere and its complex processes.
field: The atmospheric and climate effects of energetic particle precipitation.
problem: Seasonal and climate forecast models often overlook energetic particle precipitation (EPP), a missing but essential forcing mechanism that significantly influences stratospheric chemistry and dynamics, thereby affecting winter circulation patterns and regional climate.
method: This paper does not propose a new method; it is a review that synthesizes observational and modeling evidence to argue for including Energetic Particle Precipitation (EPP) forcing in climate and seasonal forecasting models to improve their accuracy.
task: The task is to review and synthesize scientific evidence on how Energetic Particle Precipitation (EPP) impacts atmospheric chemistry and dynamics, demonstrating its importance as a key forcing mechanism for climate research and seasonal forecasting.
innovation: This review synthesizes extensive evidence on how Energetic Particle Precipitation (EPP) impacts atmospheric chemistry and dynamics, arguing that it is a crucial, missing forcing that must be included in models to improve climate research and seasonal winter forecasting.

Rozanov et al. (2012) examined the combined effects of Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR), Solar Proton Events, and auroral electrons using the SOCOL v2.0 global chemistry-climate model. The study focused on how additional NOx and HOx sources influence atmospheric chemistry and dynamics. Comparing climatology with and without EPP inclusion supported the findings of Baumgaertner et al. (2011).
Using an upgraded version of the SOCOL coupled chemistry-climate model, SOCOL3-MPIOM, Arsenovic et al. (2016) investigated the effects of MEE precipitation (>30 keV) through two ensemble experiments, each with six members, for the period 2002–2010.

The term solar proton event (SPE) or solar energetic particle (SEP) event refers to proton fluxes (fluence) exceeding 10 particles cm−2 s¯¹ sr¯¹ with energies over 10 MeV (https://cdaw.gsfc.nasa.gov/CME_list/sepe/). In addition to highly energetic protons, these SEP events typically also contain highly energetic electrons up to several MeV energy. The troposphere is dynamically coupled to the variability of the stratospheric polar vortex [e.g., Baldwin and Dunkerton (1999); Baldwin et al. (2001); Scaife et al. (2016)]. For example, when the vortex strengthens, storm tracks and the tropospheric jet stream shift towards the poles (Kidston et al. 2015). Shifts in tropospheric jets are evident in the prevailing westerly winds at the polar front and are linked to variation in the Southern Annular Mode (SAM), Northern Annular Mode (NAM) (or the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)). NAM/NAO represent the leading mode of circulation variability in the northern hemisphere (Hurrell et al. 2003). Since the annular modes are closely linked to variability of the polar vortex, modulation of the stratospheric polar vortex strength or extent by EPP during winter can lead to notable surface anomalies at high latitudes, affecting pressure and temperature across North America and Eurasia.
